name: Measurements, units and uncertainties

statementText.3.1.1-02: Use of mass, length, time, amount of substance, temperature, electric current and their associated SI units.
statementText.3.1.1-04: Knowledge and use of the SI prefixes, values and standard form.
statementText.3.1.1-05: The fundamental unit of light intensity, the candela, is excluded.
statementText.3.1.1-06: Students are not expected to recall definitions of the fundamental quantities.
statementText.3.1.1-08: Students should be able to use the prefixes: T,G, M, k, c, m, μ, n, p, f,
statementText.3.1.1-09: Students should be able to convert between different units of the same quantity, eg J and eV, J and kW h.
statementText.3.1.2-02: Precision, repeatability, reproducibility, resolution and accuracy. Uncertainty:
statementText.3.1.2-04: represent uncertainty in the final answer for a quantity.
statementText.3.1.2-05: Combination of absolute and percentage uncertainties.
statementText.3.1.2-06: Represent uncertainty in a data point on a graph using error bars.
statementText.3.1.2-07: Determine the uncertainties in the gradient and intercept of a straight-line graph.
statementText.3.1.2-08: Individual points on the graph may or may not have associated error bars.
statementText.3.1.3-02: Estimation of approximate values of physical quantities.

name: Atomic structure and stable nuclei

statementText.3.2.1.1-01: Simple model of the atom, including the proton, neutron and electron. Charge and mass of the proton, neutron and electron in SI units and relative units.
statementText.3.2.1.1-02: The atomic mass unit (amu) is included in the A-level Nuclear physics section.
statementText.3.2.1.1-03: Specific charge of the proton and the electron, and of nuclei and ions.
statementText.3.2.1.1-04: Proton number Z, nucleon number A, nuclide notation.
statementText.3.2.1.1-05: Students should be familiar with the X Z A notation.
statementText.3.2.1.1-06: Meaning of isotopes and the use of isotopic data.
statementText.3.2.1.2-01: The strong nuclear force; its role in keeping the nucleus stable; short-range attraction up to approximately 3 fm, very-short range repulsion closer than approximately 0.5 fm.
statementText.3.2.1.2-02: Unstable nuclei; alpha and beta decay.
statementText.3.2.1.2-03: Equations for alpha decay, β− decay including the need for the neutrino.
statementText.3.2.1.2-04: The existence of the neutrino was hypothesised to account for conservation of energy in beta decay.

name: Particles, antiparticles and particle interactions

statementText.3.2.1.3-01: For every type of particle, there is a corresponding antiparticle.
statementText.3.2.1.3-02: Comparison of particle and antiparticle masses, charge and rest energy in MeV.
statementText.3.2.1.3-03: Students should know that the positron, antiproton, antineutron and antineutrino are the antiparticles of the electron, proton, neutron and neutrino respectively.
statementText.3.2.1.3-04: Photon model of electromagnetic radiation, the Planck constant. E = h f = hc λ
statementText.3.2.1.3-05: Knowledge of annihilation and pair production and the energies involved.
statementText.3.2.1.3-06: The use of E = mc 2 is not required in calculations.
statementText.3.2.1.4-01: Four fundamental interactions: gravity, electromagnetic, weak nuclear, strong nuclear. (The strong nuclear force may be referred to as the strong interaction.)
statementText.3.2.1.4-02: The concept of exchange particles to explain forces between elementary particles.
statementText.3.2.1.4-03: Knowledge of the gluon, Z 0 and graviton will not be tested.
statementText.3.2.1.4-04: The electromagnetic force; virtual photons as the exchange particle.
statementText.3.2.1.4-05: The weak interaction limited to β−and β + decay, electron capture and electron–proton collisions; W + and W − as the exchange particles.
statementText.3.2.1.4-06: Simple diagrams to represent the above reactions or interactions in terms of incoming and outgoing particles and exchange particles.

name: Classification of particles, quarks and conservation laws

statementText.3.2.1.5-01: Hadrons are subject to the strong interaction.
statementText.3.2.1.5-02: The two classes of hadrons: • baryons (proton, neutron) and antibaryons (antiproton and antineutron) • mesons (pion, kaon).
statementText.3.2.1.5-03: Baryon number as a quantum number.
statementText.3.2.1.5-05: The proton is the only stable baryon into which other baryons eventually decay.
statementText.3.2.1.5-06: The pion as the exchange particle of the strong nuclear force.
statementText.3.2.1.5-07: The kaon as a particle that can decay into pions.
statementText.3.2.1.5-08: Leptons: electron, muon, neutrino (electron and muon types only) and their antiparticles.
statementText.3.2.1.5-09: Lepton number as a quantum number; conservation of lepton number for muon leptons and for electron leptons.
statementText.3.2.1.5-10: The muon as a particle that decays into an electron.
statementText.3.2.1.5-12: Strange particles as particles that are produced through the strong interaction and decay through the weak interaction (eg kaons).
statementText.3.2.1.5-13: Strangeness (symbol s) as a quantum number to reflect the fact that strange particles are always created in pairs.
statementText.3.2.1.5-14: Conservation of strangeness in strong interactions.
statementText.3.2.1.5-15: Strangeness can change by 0, +1 or -1 in weak interactions.
statementText.3.2.1.5-16: Appreciation that particle physics relies on the collaborative efforts of large teams of scientists and engineers to validate new knowledge.
statementText.3.2.1.6-01: Properties of quarks and antiquarks: charge, baryon number and strangeness.
statementText.3.2.1.6-02: Combinations of quarks and antiquarks required for baryons (proton and neutron only), antibaryons (antiproton and antineutron only) and mesons (pion and kaon only).
statementText.3.2.1.6-03: Only knowledge of up (u), down (d) and strange (s) quarks and their antiquarks will be tested.
statementText.3.2.1.6-04: The decay of the neutron should be known.
statementText.3.2.1.7-01: Change of quark character in β−and in β + decay.
statementText.3.2.1.7-02: Application of the conservation laws for charge, baryon number, lepton number and strangeness to particle interactions. The necessary data will be provided in questions for particles outside those specified.
statementText.3.2.1.7-03: Students should recognise that energy and momentum are conserved in interactions.

name: The photoelectric effect

statementText.3.2.2.1-01: Threshold frequency; photon explanation of threshold frequency.
statementText.3.2.2.1-03: Photoelectric equation: h f = ϕ + Ek (max
statementText.3.2.2.1-04: Ek (max is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
statementText.3.2.2.1-05: The experimental determination of stopping potential is not required.

name: Excitation, energy levels and wave-particle duality

statementText.3.2.2.2-01: Ionisation and excitation; understanding of ionisation and excitation in the fluorescent tube.
statementText.3.2.2.2-03: Students will be expected to be able to convert eV into J and vice versa.
statementText.3.2.2.3-01: Line spectra (eg of atomic hydrogen) as evidence for transitions between discrete energy levels in atoms. h f = E1 −E2
statementText.3.2.2.3-02: In questions, energy levels may be quoted in J or eV.
statementText.3.2.2.4-01: Students should know that electron diffraction suggests that particles possess wave properties and the photoelectric effect suggests that electromagnetic waves have a particulate nature.
statementText.3.2.2.4-02: Details of particular methods of particle diffraction are not expected.
statementText.3.2.2.4-03: de Broglie wavelength λ = h mv where mv is the momentum.
statementText.3.2.2.4-04: Students should be able to explain how and why the amount of diffraction changes when the momentum of the particle is changed.
statementText.3.2.2.4-05: Appreciation of how knowledge and understanding of the nature of matter changes over time.
statementText.3.2.2.4-06: Appreciation that such changes need to be evaluated through peer review and validated by the scientific community.

name: Progressive waves, longitudinal and transverse waves

statementText.3.3.1.1-01: Oscillation of the particles of the medium;
statementText.3.3.1.1-02: amplitude, frequency, wavelength, speed, phase, phase difference, c = f λ f = 1 T
statementText.3.3.1.1-03: Phase difference may be measured as angles (radians and degrees) or as fractions of a cycle.
statementText.3.3.1.2-01: Nature of longitudinal and transverse waves.
statementText.3.3.1.2-02: Examples to include: sound, electromagnetic waves, and waves on a string.
statementText.3.3.1.2-03: Students will be expected to know the direction of displacement of particles/fields relative to the direction of energy propagation and that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
statementText.3.3.1.2-04: Polarisation as evidence for the nature of transverse waves.
statementText.3.3.1.2-05: Applications of polarisers to include Polaroid material and the alignment of aerials for transmission and reception.
statementText.3.3.1.2-06: Malus’s law will not be expected.

name: Superposition and stationary waves

statementText.3.3.1.3-02: Nodes and antinodes on strings. f = 1 2l T μ for first harmonic.
statementText.3.3.1.3-03: The formation of stationary waves by two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions.
statementText.3.3.1.3-04: A graphical explanation of formation of stationary waves will be expected.
statementText.3.3.1.3-05: Stationary waves formed on a string and those produced with microwaves and sound waves should be considered.
statementText.3.3.1.3-06: Stationary waves on strings will be described in terms of harmonics. The terms fundamental (for first harmonic) and overtone will not be used.
statementText.3.3.1.3-07: Required practical 1: Investigation into the variation of the frequency of stationary waves on a string with length, tension and mass per unit length of the string.

name: Interference, diffraction and the diffraction grating

statementText.3.3.2.1-02: Interference and diffraction using a laser as a source of monochromatic light.
statementText.3.3.2.1-03: Young’s double-slit experiment: the use of two coherent sources or the use of a single source with double slits to produce an interference pattern.
statementText.3.3.2.1-05: Production of interference pattern using white light.
statementText.3.3.2.1-06: Students are expected to show awareness of safety issues associated with using lasers.
statementText.3.3.2.1-07: Students will not be required to describe how a laser works.
statementText.3.3.2.1-08: Students will be expected to describe and explain interference produced with sound and electromagnetic waves.
statementText.3.3.2.1-09: Appreciation of how knowledge and understanding of nature of electromagnetic radiation has changed over time.
statementText.3.3.2.1-10: Required practical 2: Investigation of interference effects to include the Young’s slit experiment and interference by a diffraction grating.
statementText.3.3.2.2-01: Appearance of the diffraction pattern from a single slit using monochromatic and white light.
statementText.3.3.2.2-02: Qualitative treatment of the variation of the width of the central diffraction maximum with wavelength and slit width. The graph of intensity against angular separation is not required.
statementText.3.3.2.2-03: Plane transmission diffraction grating at normal incidence.
statementText.3.3.2.2-05: Use of the spectrometer will not be tested.

name: Refraction, total internal reflection and optical fibres

statementText.3.3.2.3-01: Refractive index of a substance, n = c cs
statementText.3.3.2.3-02: Students should recall that the refractive index of air is approximately 1.
statementText.3.3.2.3-03: Snell’s law of refraction for a boundary n1sinθ1 = n2sinθ2
statementText.3.3.2.3-04: Total internal reflection sinθc = n2 n1
statementText.3.3.2.3-05: Simple treatment of fibre optics including the function of the cladding.
statementText.3.3.2.3-06: Optical fibres will be limited to step index only.
statementText.3.3.2.3-08: Students are expected to understand the principles and consequences of pulse broadening and absorption.

name: Scalars, vectors and moments

statementText.3.4.1.1-04: Addition of vectors by calculation or scale drawing.
statementText.3.4.1.1-05: Calculations will be limited to two vectors at right angles. Scale drawings may involve vectors at angles other than 90°.
statementText.3.4.1.1-06: Resolution of vectors into two components at right angles to each other.
statementText.3.4.1.1-07: Examples should include components of forces along and perpendicular to an inclined plane.
statementText.3.4.1.1-08: Problems may be solved either by the use of resolved forces or the use of a closed triangle.
statementText.3.4.1.1-09: Conditions for equilibrium for two or three coplanar forces acting at a point. Appreciation of the meaning of equilibrium in the context of an object at rest or moving with constant velocity.
statementText.3.4.1.2-01: Moment of a force about a point.
statementText.3.4.1.2-02: Moment defined as force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
statementText.3.4.1.2-03: Couple as a pair of equal and opposite coplanar forces.
statementText.3.4.1.2-04: Moment of couple defined as force × perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces.
statementText.3.4.1.2-07: Knowledge that the position of the centre of mass of uniform regular solid is at its centre.

name: Motion along a straight line and projectile motion

statementText.3.4.1.3-01: Displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration. v = ∆s ∆t a = ∆v ∆t
statementText.3.4.1.3-02: Calculations may include average and instantaneous speeds and velocities.
statementText.3.4.1.3-03: Representation by graphical methods of uniform and non- uniform acceleration.
statementText.3.4.1.3-04: Significance of areas of velocity–time and acceleration– time graphs and gradients of displacement–time and velocity–time graphs for uniform and non-uniform acceleration eg graphs for motion of bouncing ball.
statementText.3.4.1.3-05: Equations for uniform acceleration: v = u + at s = u + v 2 t s = ut + at2 2 v 2 = u 2 + 2as
statementText.3.4.1.3-07: Required practical 3: Determination of g by a freefall method.
statementText.3.4.1.4-01: Independent effect of motion in horizontal and vertical directions of a uniform gravitational field. Problems will be solvable using the equations of uniform acceleration.
statementText.3.4.1.4-03: Distinctions between static and dynamic friction will not be tested.
statementText.3.4.1.4-04: Qualitative treatment of lift and drag forces.
statementText.3.4.1.4-06: Knowledge that air resistance increases with speed.
statementText.3.4.1.4-07: Qualitative understanding of the effect of air resistance on the trajectory of a projectile and on the factors that affect the maximum speed of a vehicle.

name: Newton's laws of motion and momentum

statementText.3.4.1.5-01: Knowledge and application of the three laws of motion in appropriate situations. F = ma for situations where the mass is constant.
statementText.3.4.1.6-03: Principle applied quantitatively to problems in one dimension.
statementText.3.4.1.6-04: Force as the rate of change of momentum, F = ∆mv ∆t
statementText.3.4.1.6-05: Impulse = change in momentum F∆t = ∆mv , where F is constant.
statementText.3.4.1.6-06: Significance of the area under a force–time graph.
statementText.3.4.1.6-07: Quantitative questions may be set on forces that vary with time. Impact forces are related to contact times (eg kicking a football, crumple zones, packaging).
statementText.3.4.1.6-09: Appreciation of momentum conservation issues in the context of ethical transport design.

name: Work, energy, power and conservation of energy

statementText.3.4.1.7-01: Energy transferred, W = Fscosθ rate of doing work = rate of energy transfer, P = ∆W ∆t = Fv
statementText.3.4.1.7-02: Quantitative questions may be set on variable forces.
statementText.3.4.1.7-03: Significance of the area under a force–displacement graph. efficiency = useful output power input power
statementText.3.4.1.7-04: Efficiency can be expressed as a percentage.
statementText.3.4.1.8-01: Principle of conservation of energy. ∆Ep = mg∆h and Ek = 1 2mv 2
statementText.3.4.1.8-02: Quantitative and qualitative application of energy conservation to examples involving gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and work done against resistive forces.

name: Materials, stress, strain and the Young modulus

statementText.3.4.2.1-02: Hooke’s law, elastic limit, F = k∆L , k as stiffness and spring constant.
statementText.3.4.2.1-05: energy stored = 1 2F∆L = area under force−extension graph
statementText.3.4.2.1-06: Description of plastic behaviour, fracture and brittle behaviour linked to force–extension graphs.
statementText.3.4.2.1-07: Quantitative and qualitative application of energy conservation to examples involving elastic strain energy and energy to deform.
statementText.3.4.2.1-08: Spring energy transformed to kinetic and gravitational potential energy.
statementText.3.4.2.1-10: Appreciation of energy conservation issues in the context of ethical transport design.
statementText.3.4.2.2-01: Young modulus = tensile stress tensile strain = A ∆L FL
statementText.3.4.2.2-02: Use of stress–strain graphs to find the Young modulus.
statementText.3.4.2.2-03: (One simple method of measurement is required.)
statementText.3.4.2.2-04: Required practical 4: Determination of the Young modulus by a simple method.

name: Current, potential difference, I-V characteristics and resistivity

statementText.3.5.1.1-01: Electric current as the rate of flow of charge; potential difference as work done per unit charge. I = ∆Q ∆t , V = W Q
statementText.3.5.1.1-02: Resistance defined as R = V I
statementText.3.5.1.2-01: For an ohmic conductor, semiconductor diode, and filament lamp.
statementText.3.5.1.2-02: Ohm’s law as a special case where I ∝V under constant physical conditions.
statementText.3.5.1.2-03: Unless specifically stated in questions, ammeters and voltmeters should be treated as ideal (having zero and infinite resistance respectively).
statementText.3.5.1.2-04: Questions can be set where either I or V is on the horizontal axis of the characteristic graph.
statementText.3.5.1.3-02: Description of the qualitative effect of temperature on the resistance of metal conductors and thermistors.
statementText.3.5.1.3-03: Only negative temperature coefficient (ntc) thermistors will be considered.
statementText.3.5.1.3-04: Applications of thermistors to include temperature sensors and resistance–temperature graphs.
statementText.3.5.1.3-05: Superconductivity as a property of certain materials which have zero resistivity at and below a critical temperature which depends on the material.
statementText.3.5.1.3-06: Applications of superconductors to include the production of strong magnetic fields and the reduction of energy loss in transmission of electric power.
statementText.3.5.1.3-07: Critical field will not be assessed.
statementText.3.5.1.3-08: Required practical 5: Determination of resistivity of a wire using a micrometer, ammeter and voltmeter.

name: Circuits and potential dividers

statementText.3.5.1.4-01: Resistors: in series, RT = R1 + R2 + R3 + … in parallel, 1 RT = 1 R1 + 1 R2 + 1 R3 + … Energy and power equations: E = IVt; P = IV = I 2R = V R 2
statementText.3.5.1.4-02: The relationships between currents, voltages and resistances in series and parallel circuits, including cells in series and identical cells in parallel.
statementText.3.5.1.4-03: Conservation of charge and conservation of energy in dc circuits.
statementText.3.5.1.5-01: The potential divider used to supply constant or variable potential difference from a power supply.
statementText.3.5.1.5-02: The use of the potentiometer as a measuring instrument is not required.
statementText.3.5.1.5-03: Examples should include the use of variable resistors, thermistors, and light dependent resistors (LDR) in the potential divider.

name: Electromotive force and internal resistance

statementText.3.5.1.6-01: ε = E Q , ε = I R + r
statementText.3.5.1.6-03: Students will be expected to understand and perform calculations for circuits in which the internal resistance of the supply is not negligible.
statementText.3.5.1.6-04: Required practical 6: Investigation of the emf and internal resistance of electric cells and batteries by measuring the variation of the terminal pd of the cell with current in it.

name: Circular motion

statementText.3.6.1.1-01: Motion in a circular path at constant speed implies there is an acceleration and requires a centripetal force.
statementText.3.6.1.1-02: Magnitude of angular speed ω = v r = 2π f
statementText.3.6.1.1-04: Direction of angular velocity will not be considered.
statementText.3.6.1.1-05: Centripetal acceleration a = v2 r = ω 2r
statementText.3.6.1.1-06: The derivation of the centripetal acceleration formula will not be examined.
statementText.3.6.1.1-07: Centripetal force F = mv2 r = mω 2r

name: Simple harmonic motion, forced vibrations and resonance

statementText.3.6.1.2-01: Analysis of characteristics of simple harmonic motion (SHM).
statementText.3.6.1.2-03: Defining equation: a = −ω 2x x = Acosωt and v = ± ω A 2 −x 2
statementText.3.6.1.2-04: Graphical representations linking the variations of x, v and a with time.
statementText.3.6.1.2-05: Appreciation that the v −t graph is derived from the gradient of the x −t graph and that the a −t graph is derived from the gradient of the v −t graph.
statementText.3.6.1.3-01: Study of mass-spring system: T = 2π m k
statementText.3.6.1.3-02: Study of simple pendulum: T = 2π g l
statementText.3.6.1.3-03: Questions may involve other harmonic oscillators (eg liquid in U-tube) but full information will be provided in questions where necessary.
statementText.3.6.1.3-04: Variation of Ek, Ep, and total energy with both displacement and time.
statementText.3.6.1.3-06: Required practical 7: Investigation into simple harmonic motion using a mass–spring system and a simple pendulum.
statementText.3.6.1.4-01: Qualitative treatment of free and forced vibrations.
statementText.3.6.1.4-02: Resonance and the effects of damping on the sharpness of resonance.
statementText.3.6.1.4-03: Examples of these effects in mechanical systems and situations involving stationary waves.

name: Thermal energy transfer and ideal gases

statementText.3.6.2.1-01: Internal energy is the sum of the randomly distributed kinetic energies and potential energies of the particles in a body.
statementText.3.6.2.1-02: The internal energy of a system is increased when energy is transferred to it by heating or when work is done on it (and vice versa), eg a qualitative treatment of the first law of thermodynamics.
statementText.3.6.2.1-03: Appreciation that during a change of state the potential energies of the particle ensemble are changing but not the kinetic energies. Calculations involving transfer of energy.
statementText.3.6.2.1-04: For a change of temperature: Q = mc ∆θ where c is specific heat capacity.
statementText.3.6.2.1-06: For a change of state Q = ml where l is the specific latent heat.
statementText.3.6.2.2-01: Gas laws as experimental relationships between p, V, T and the mass of the gas.
statementText.3.6.2.2-02: Concept of absolute zero of temperature.
statementText.3.6.2.2-03: Ideal gas equation: pV = nRT for n moles and pV = NkT for N molecules. Work done = p∆V
statementText.3.6.2.2-04: Avogadro constant NA, molar gas constant R, Boltzmann constant k
statementText.3.6.2.2-06: Required practical 8: Investigation of Boyle's law (constant temperature) and Charles’s law (constant pressure) for a gas.

name: Molecular kinetic theory

statementText.3.6.2.3-01: Brownian motion as evidence for existence of atoms.
statementText.3.6.2.3-02: Explanation of relationships between p, V and T in terms of a simple molecular model.
statementText.3.6.2.3-03: Students should understand that the gas laws are empirical in nature whereas the kinetic theory model arises from theory.
statementText.3.6.2.3-04: Assumptions leading to pV = 1 3Nm crms 2 including derivation of the equation and calculations.
statementText.3.6.2.3-05: A simple algebraic approach involving conservation of momentum is required.
statementText.3.6.2.3-06: Appreciation that for an ideal gas internal energy is kinetic energy of the atoms.
statementText.3.6.2.3-07: Use of average molecular kinetic energy = 1 2 = 3 2m crms 2kT = 3RT 2NA
statementText.3.6.2.3-08: Appreciation of how knowledge and understanding of the behaviour of a gas has changed over time.

name: Gravitational fields and orbits

statementText.3.7.1-01: Concept of a force field as a region in which a body experiences a non-contact force.
statementText.3.7.1-02: Students should recognise that a force field can be represented as a vector, the direction of which must be determined by inspection.
statementText.3.7.1-03: Force fields arise from the interaction of mass, of static charge, and between moving charges.
statementText.3.7.1-04: Similarities and differences between gravitational and electrostatic forces:
statementText.3.7.1-05: Similarities: Both have inverse-square force laws that have many characteristics in common, eg use of field lines, use of potential concept, equipotential surfaces etc
statementText.3.7.1-06: Differences: masses always attract, but charges may attract or repel
statementText.3.7.2.1-01: Gravity as a universal attractive force acting between all matter.
statementText.3.7.2.1-02: Magnitude of force between point masses: F = Gm1m2 r2
statementText.3.7.2.1-03: where G is the gravitational constant.
statementText.3.7.2.2-01: Representation of a gravitational field by gravitational field lines. g as force per unit mass as defined by g = F m
statementText.3.7.2.2-02: Magnitude of g in a radial field given by g = GM r2
statementText.3.7.2.3-01: Understanding of definition of gravitational potential, including zero value at infinity.
statementText.3.7.2.3-03: Work done in moving mass m given by ∆W = m∆V
statementText.3.7.2.3-05: Idea that no work is done when moving along an equipotential surface. V in a radial field given by V = −GM r
statementText.3.7.2.3-07: Graphical representations of variations of g and V with r. V related to g by: g = −∆V ∆r ∆V from area under graph of g against r.
statementText.3.7.2.4-01: Orbital period and speed related to radius of circular orbit; derivation of T2 ∝r3
statementText.3.7.2.4-02: Energy considerations for an orbiting satellite.
statementText.3.7.2.4-03: Total energy of an orbiting satellite.
statementText.3.7.2.4-06: Use of satellites in low orbits and geostationary orbits, to include plane and radius of geostationary orbit.

name: Electric fields and electric potential

statementText.3.7.3.1-01: Force between point charges in a vacuum: F = 4πε0 1 Q1Q2 r2
statementText.3.7.3.1-03: Appreciation that air can be treated as a vacuum when calculating force between charges.
statementText.3.7.3.1-04: For a charged sphere, charge may be considered to be at the centre.
statementText.3.7.3.1-05: Comparison of magnitude of gravitational and electrostatic forces between subatomic particles.
statementText.3.7.3.2-01: Representation of electric fields by electric field lines.
statementText.3.7.3.2-02: Electric field strength. E as force per unit charge defined by E = F Q
statementText.3.7.3.2-03: Magnitude of E in a uniform field given by E = V d
statementText.3.7.3.2-04: Derivation from work done moving charge between plates: Fd = QΔV
statementText.3.7.3.2-05: Trajectory of moving charged particle entering a uniform electric field initially at right angles.
statementText.3.7.3.2-06: Magnitude of E in a radial field given by E = 4πε0 1 r2 Q
statementText.3.7.3.3-01: Understanding of definition of absolute electric potential, including zero value at infinity, and of electric potential difference.
statementText.3.7.3.3-02: Work done in moving charge Q given by ∆W = Q ∆V

statementText.3.13.6.4-12: The AS specification is designed to be taken over one or two years with all assessments taken at the end of the course. The A-level specification is designed to be taken over two years with all assessments taken at the end of the course.
statementText.3.13.6.4-13: Assessments and certification for the AS specification are available for the first time in May/June and then every May/June for the life of the specification.
statementText.3.13.6.4-14: Assessments and certification for the A-level specification are available for the first time in May/ June and then every May/June for the life of the specification.
statementText.3.13.6.4-15: These are linear qualifications. In order to achieve the award, students must complete all exams in May/June in a single year. All assessments must be taken in the same series.
statementText.3.13.6.4-16: Questions for these specifications will be set which require students to demonstrate: • their knowledge and understanding of the content developed in one section or topic, including the associated mathematical and practical skills or • the ability to apply mathematical and practical skills to areas of content they are not normally developed in or • the ability to draw together different areas of knowledge and understanding within one answer.
statementText.3.13.6.4-17: A range of question types will be used, including those that require extended responses. Extended response questions will allow students to demonstrate their ability to construct and develop a sustained line of reasoning which is coherent, relevant, substantiated and logically structured. Extended responses may be in written English, extended calculations, or a combination of both, as appropriate to the question.
statementText.3.13.6.4-18: All materials are available in English only. 4.1 Aims
statementText.3.13.6.4-19: Courses based on these specifications should encourage students to: • develop their interest in and enthusiasm for the subject, including developing an interest in further study and careers associated with the subject • develop essential knowledge and understanding of different areas of the subject and how they relate to each other • develop and demonstrate a deep appreciation of the skills, knowledge and understanding of scientific methods • develop competence and confidence in a variety of practical, mathematical and problem solving skills • understand how society makes decisions about scientific issues and how the sciences contribute to the success of the economy and society • use theories, models and ideas to develop scientific explanations • use knowledge and understanding to pose scientific questions, define scientific problems, present scientific arguments and scientific ideas
